rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and reveal the overall elution window and any critical pairs. This balances coverage and resolution without being so shallow that late compounds risk missing the 42 min cutoff.

All compounds eluted cleanly and early, so trim the gradient window to the actual elution region to improve efficiency and likely reduce run time while keeping all peaks inside the gradient. This also tests whether the critical cluster around rows 5 to 7 benefits from a narrower, more focused phi range at the same slope duration and temperature.

The broad window at 40 C already gave perfect resolution, so now exploit time by keeping the successful phi range but halving tG to compress the chromatogram. This directly tests how much of the current excess resolution margin can be traded for a shorter run while watching the rows 5 to 7 cluster.

The 10 min gradient is very fast but over-compresses the critical 5 to 7 cluster, while 20 min had ample resolution; an intermediate tG should recover that pair without reintroducing a time penalty. This is the quickest way to locate the resolution-time optimum around the current best method.

The optimum is clearly between 14 and 20 min, and the only remaining weakness is the 6/7 pair; a modest increase in tG from 14 to 16 min should selectively gain resolution with essentially no time penalty. This refines the slope near the current best method before exploring temperature effects.

Since 14 min is near-optimal in slope, use temperature to target the persistent 6/7 pair that may not respond strongly to tG. A 5 C decrease should modestly shift selectivity and may separate that pair while likely keeping the run short enough to avoid any time penalty.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by moving the critical overlap from 6/7 to 5/6, so test the opposite direction at the same near-optimal gradient. A 5 C increase may improve selectivity for the crowded mid-cluster without adding time penalty.

Since 15 min is unavailable on the grid and 16 min slightly overpaid in time while 14 min under-resolved the critical pair, probe farther toward the high-resolution side with 18 min. This checks whether the scoring function favors full resolution strongly enough to offset a modest time penalty.

All peaks elute by about phi_e 0.46 in the best run, so the current upper endpoint is far above the useful window; slightly lowering phi1 should make the effective gradient shallower in the occupied region and may improve the 6/7 pair without much increasing run time. This tests phi-window tuning while keeping the best tG and temperature fixed.

The slight reduction of phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved CRF, so continue trimming the upper endpoint toward the actual elution window to further shallow the useful gradient. This may push the critical 6/7 pair just over the target while likely remaining under the time-penalty threshold.

Injection 9 is nearly optimal with no time penalty but still slightly under-resolves the 6/7 pair; a shorter tG on the improved phi window will show whether CRF is driven more by speed or by that residual resolution deficit. This helps bracket the local optimum around the new best window.

With the improved phi1 = 0.90 window, test whether a slightly longer gradient than the current best can fully resolve the 6/7 pair while staying below the time-penalty threshold. This is the most direct refinement around the present optimum after 12 min proved too steep.

At phi1 = 0.90 and tG = 14, only a small selectivity improvement is needed to beat the current best, so re-test temperature on the improved window. Since temperature strongly altered which pair was critical before, a 5 C decrease could favorably reshape the central cluster without incurring a time penalty.

At the improved phi window, complete the temperature bracket around the current best by testing 45 C since 35 C worsened the central selectivity. If 45 C shifts the crowded cluster in the favorable direction, it could convert the slight 6/7 deficit into a fully resolved separation with no time penalty.

Temperature is clearly inferior to 40 C, so return to the best selectivity and continue trimming phi1 toward the actual elution range. The 0.85 run achieved full baseline resolution but incurred only a tiny time penalty, so 0.80 may reveal whether the score can be improved by a small further gain in resolution or if 0.90 is the true optimum.

The main remaining uncertainty is whether a different temperature can be rescued by a shallower gradient, since temperature alone at 14 min strongly changed which pair overlaps. This run probes a possible interaction between T and slope that could improve the crowded middle cluster, while still keeping all analytes safely within the gradient.

The first peak in the best method is still fairly early, so raising phi0 slightly may compress only the uncritical front of the chromatogram while shifting the useful gradient window upward toward the crowded mid-elution region. This tests whether the same overall width but a repositioned phi window can improve the 6/7 selectivity without adding time penalty.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved the score, so now combine that gain with a slight reduction in phi1 to make the active gradient a bit shallower over the crowded central region. This could nudge the 6/7 pair over the apparent threshold while keeping the last peak early enough to avoid a time penalty.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so use remaining injections only to map robustness around the optimum and guard against a narrow sweet spot. Increasing phi0 slightly while holding the successful phi1, tG, and T tests whether the perfect score sits on a broad plateau or drops off quickly.

We already have two perfect methods, so continue defining the robust high-scoring region by stepping phi0 upward. This will show how far the lower endpoint can be raised before the earliest compounds become overly compressed or approach unretained behavior.

The best region now appears centered near phi0 0.10 to 0.15 and phi1 0.85, so test whether trimming phi1 slightly further at the successful higher phi0 preserves full resolution while shortening the late tail. This maps the edge of the perfect-score plateau in the most promising local neighborhood.

Two perfect methods suggest a broad optimum, so test the missing corner between them by pairing phi0 0.10 with phi1 0.80 at the same tG and temperature. This will complete the local response surface around the optimum and confirm whether the plateau extends diagonally across both endpoint settings.

The perfect-score plateau seems centered at phi0 0.10 to 0.15 and phi1 0.85, so test the remaining neighboring combination with a slightly higher phi1 at the successful phi0 = 0.15. This completes the local map and checks whether 0.85 is truly the optimal upper bound or just one point on a flat ridge.

With the optimum region mapped and CRF already at 1.000, use a remaining injection to test robustness to a faster method anchored at one perfect endpoint set. This checks whether the perfect window still performs acceptably at shorter tG for potential throughput gains, while avoiding any duplicate of prior runs.

For the final run, test the faster version of the other perfect-scoring endpoint set to complete the local robustness picture around the optimum. This determines whether raising phi0 to 0.15 better preserves the critical 6/7 resolution at shorter tG than the phi0 0.10 version did.
